prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active forms of the incretin hormone GLP-1 that made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six of us placed GLP-1 first, and I still think that is the right call on scientific grounds and not only because of the unanimity. The chain runs from proglucagon processing and the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, through its glucose-dependent insulinotropic and satiety actions in humans, to the realization that protease-resistant agonists could be drugs. It has been independently confirmed for decades, supported by large randomized outcome trials, and now affects glycemic control, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes in very large populations. Few candidates combine this originality, mechanistic clarity and patient impact, and the maturity question is settled. My preferred trio is Holst (human physiology and secretion), Drucker (receptor biology, proglucagon-derived peptides, therapeutic concept) and Mojsov (identification and synthesis of the active peptide), because a prize citation framed around the discovery of the hormone's active form and its physiology is the most scientifically defensible reading of the credit record.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Mojsov's priority is publicly contested, in particular against the Habener group, which is not among the credited names, so naming her risks crediting a disputed claim while excluding a competing one. Leaving out Lotte Bjerre Knudsen means a prize for the discovery arc that omits the person who led the long-acting analogues (liraglutide, semaglutide) which actually delivered the clinical impact. Either trio can therefore be criticized as unfair, and four credited names cannot fit into three places. A further concern is that a physiology-only citation may seem to underweight the translational step on which the public-health impact depends.

responses.point: El-Manira ranks GLP-1 first but proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, leaving out Mojsov because the weight of her contribution is disputed, and treating Knudsen as the pharmacological step that gave durable long-acting agonists.
responses.response: I take the Mojsov problem seriously and agree that her weight is not settled by the supplied record. But I do not think the answer is to substitute a drug-development credit for a discovery credit. The sequence of proglucagon processing, identification of GLP-1(7-36) amide and its human physiology is the discovery that the drugs rest on. Knudsen's work is a major pharmaceutical achievement on top of that, and I would not object to it if the committee wants the citation to cover translation, but I would then want the citation to say so explicitly, and I would want the committee to examine whether Mojsov or Knudsen has the stronger independent claim before we commit. I do not yet regard this as resolved in either direction.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that a prize here would recognize both mechanism and translation, so Knudsen's development of liraglutide and semaglutide belongs with Drucker and Holst, with Mojsov left out because her credit is contested.
responses.response: I agree that mechanism plus translation is what makes this case so strong, and that excluding Knudsen is a real fairness question and not a technicality. Where I differ is that I would not let contested priority push out the person who identified the active peptide form on the grounds of uncertainty alone. If the dispute with the Habener group is the issue, it applies to Mojsov and affects who else might belong, not Knudsen. I accept that if the committee prefers a mechanism-to-medicine citation, Drucker, Holst and Knudsen is a coherent trio, and I hold my preference only loosely.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, omits Knudsen as an industrial drug-development contributor, ranks CAR-T second (June and Sadelain) and the unfolded protein response third.
responses.response: We agree on the trio and on Knudsen being the hard exclusion. I would qualify the reason: the prize record includes drug-development work, so her exclusion should rest on the weight of her independent scientific contribution and not on where it was done. I also differ on CAR-T, which I did not rank, mainly because the foundational chimeric-receptor concept is incompletely credited without Eshhar and the credited trio does not map cleanly onto the early-design versus clinical-translation split that you draw. I would pressure-test that rather than treat it as a safe second choice.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and optogenetics second, noting that six credited names exceed the three-laureate limit and any trio omits Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck.
responses.response: I agree on GLP-1 and on the trio. On optogenetics, I put it fifth, and the reason is not a doubt about its originality or reach but that the credit is the least tractable of the shortlist: channelrhodopsin discovery and neuronal deployment are separable achievements, and a three-person cap forces an exclusion that I think would be contested for years. I also give some weight to the point that it is a tool, so the committee has to decide whether a method prize is competitive with a mechanism-to-therapy discovery. I would keep it as a candidate but not as a challenger to GLP-1 this year.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks GLP-1 first with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, calls Knudsen a credible alternative, and ranks UPR and optogenetics next, and treats cGAS-STING as a lower-ranked but solid mechanism.
responses.response: I agree with your GLP-1 reading, including that the split between basic hormone biology and drug development is unresolved. On cGAS-STING we are close on the core pair of Chen and Barber, but I would be more cautious on timing: the biology is solid, yet STING agonists and antagonists have not produced a validated therapy, so I would put it behind UPR for this year even though I find it compelling for autoimmunity.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's claim, relative to the Habener group and to Knudsen, is strong enough to place her in the trio; the credit record supplied does not settle it.
Whether the committee wants a physiology-only citation or one that also covers drug development, which determines whether Knudsen belongs.

Whether the unfolded protein response, which I value highly, should be preferred over GLP-1 in a later year if the committee wants to spread recognition across fields; I currently do not think it should compete with GLP-1 this year.
Whether cGAS-STING will gain clinical validation soon enough to change its maturity assessment.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My research is in autoimmunity, Sjögren's disease and Ro52/TRIM21, and none of the credited names for B043, B010 or B049 is among my recorded co-authors (Kuchroo, Sonesson); a topical interest in nucleic-acid sensing or a shared KI setting is not a personal tie.
